# My workflow
N = 1, and these are opinions

## The loop, per milestone

::: {.flow}
::: {.panel .compact}
**1 · Spec**

What does this milestone build? Theory and working equations.
Where is domain knowledge essential? Which invariants and limits can we test?

[Human writes / approves]{.accent-strong}
:::

::: {.panel .compact}
**2 · Tests first**

Tests implemented before any code.
Check they fail, then review them.

[Human gate: review tests]{.accent-strong}
:::

::: {.panel .compact}
**3 · Implement**

The agent implements against the tests and the spec.
:::

::: {.panel .compact}
**4 · Validate & review**

A Quarto validation document runs the code on a real example
as an integration test. Then code review.

[Human gate: review results and code]{.accent-strong}
:::
:::

::: {.wide}
[Nguyen: set up, then step in when stuck. Here: a human gate on every milestone.]{.muted}
:::

::: notes
The spec step is where I decide where the domain knowledge sits: exactly the
places the cases showed agents fail (the Bloch phase sign, electron count, alpha).
Reviewing the tests before implementation matters because if the agent writes both
tests and code, they can quietly fit each other, which is the alpha = 0.27 pattern.
:::

## Reviewability is the product

The hard part is getting code from the agent that you can **review**.

My criterion: reviewing it should be **faster than writing it yourself**.

::: {.panel .compact .wide}
O'Brien et al. (2025), survey of 868 scientists who program: the strongest single predictor
of *feeling* productive with AI tools was **how many lines of generated code people accept at once**.
Small in absolute terms (~10% of variance), but larger than any other factor.

[Their reading: scientists may gauge productivity by code generation rather than validation.]{.muted}
:::

::: notes
METR's randomized trial points the same way: experienced developers estimated AI made
them 20% faster, but it made them 19% slower (early-2025 tools, large mature codebases).
Feeling productive and being productive can come apart.
What makes code reviewable for me: small milestones, tests reviewed before code,
a validation document showing the code on a real problem, and the tooling on the next slide.
:::

## Project scaffolding

::: {.compact .wide}
| Tier | Tools | Signal |
|---|---|---|
| **Must have** | git | What changed, and a way back |
| | pixi or uv | Same environment for agent, you and CI |
| | pytest | Does the code do what the tests say? |
| **Too cheap to skip** | ruff, mypy | Style and common bugs; types and interfaces |
| **High value for scientific code** | Quarto, hypothesis | Readable results on real examples; invariants over many inputs |
| **When you need more confidence** | jaxtyping, mutmut | Array shapes and dtypes; can the tests actually fail? |
:::

::: {.wide}
[Each tool is a signal to **both** the agent and the human. They only help if they run on every change: `CLAUDE.md`, hooks, pre-commit, CI.]{.muted}
:::

::: notes
hypothesis is the natural way to encode the invariants from the spec: electron count,
Hermiticity, symmetries, limits. Those are exactly the checks AInsteinBench says the
agent lacked.
mutmut answers the "tests too loose" failure: if mutating the code doesn't break a test,
the test isn't checking much.
:::

## How this maps to the evidence

::: {.compact .wide}
| Practice | Supported by | Complicated by / open |
|---|---|---|
| Spec names invariants, limits, where domain knowledge matters | Failures sit exactly there (AInsteinBench C.8, C.9; Nguyen's α) | — |
| Tests first, reviewed | Oracle tests drove 10 of 15 fixes (Nguyen) | Tests can be too loose or too strict (AInsteinBench §5.2): hence the review |
| Validation on a real example | Single-point tests hid α (Nguyen) | One example is still one point |
| Small milestones with human gates | 33 stuck sessions (Nguyen); success comes early (AInsteinBench §4.3) | No study compares gated and hands-off workflows |
| Reviewability as the goal | Perceived productivity tracks lines accepted (O'Brien) | How to measure reviewability is open |
:::
